title: const, constexpr, and Where a Value Lives
summary: Tell run-time constants from compile-time ones, see where each value ends up, and share constants between files with inline constexpr instead of macros.
intro: A trading program is full of fixed numbers: a tick size, a lot size, a fee rate, the depth of a book. Some are known when you write the code, and some only once the program starts. C++ has a keyword for each: `const` promises a value won't change, and `constexpr` promises the compiler knows it. This lesson shows where each one is allowed, where the value ends up (inside an instruction, in read-only data, or on the stack), and how to share a constant between files with the linkage rules from *Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker*.

steps.title: const: read-only, set at run time

example.title: A start-of-day order limit
example.prompt: Compute an order limit from the desk's positions when the program runs, keep it const, and check three orders against it.
example.explanation: `orderLimit` gets its value from a function call, so nobody knows it until the program runs, yet it is just as `const` as a literal. The positions add to 450,000, and 10% of that is 45,000. Inside the loop, `order` reads each element through a `const` name, and `ok` is `const` too, because nothing changes it after it's set. Every variable in `main` is `const`, which tells a reader at a glance that nothing here moves once it's computed.

practice.title: A spread alert
practice.prompt:
Compute an alert threshold from the day's quotes at run time, keep it const, and flag the wide spreads.

1. Declare `const double average` from `averageSpread(spreads)` and `const double alertAbove` as twice the average.
2. Print `average: ` with the average, then `alert above: ` with the threshold.
3. For each spread, print it followed by ` wide` when it is above `alertAbove`, and ` ok` otherwise.

Expected output:

```text
average: 4.00
alert above: 8.00
2 ok
3 ok
2 ok
9 wide
4 ok
```

tests.output:
average: 4.00
alert above: 8.00
2 ok
3 ok
2 ok
9 wide
4 ok

hints: A `const` can be initialized from a call: `const double average = averageSpread(spreads);`.
The spreads are `int`s and print without decimals. Only the two doubles show the 2 places.

steps.title: constexpr: known while compiling
steps.body:
A few places in C++ need a value the compiler knows while it compiles, a **constant expression**: the size of a C array, the `N` in `std::array<double, N>` (a **template argument**, which becomes part of the type), and every `case` label. A `const` set at run time can't go there:

```cpp error
const std::vector<double> prices = {101.25, 101.26, 101.24};
const int n = static_cast<int>(prices.size());
std::array<double, n> copy{};
std::cout << copy.size() << '\n';
```

g++ says `error: the value of 'n' is not usable in a constant expression` with `note: 'n' was not initialized with a constant expression`.

**`constexpr`** declares a constant that must be computed while compiling. If the compiler can't, the declaration itself is the error, right where you wrote it: `constexpr int n = prices.size();` fails with `call to non-'constexpr' function`. So `constexpr` both says and checks that a value is settled before the program runs. Constants here are named `kName`, as in *Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker*, and the last part says why.

Two old rules blur the line. A `const int` set from a literal also counts as a constant expression, but a `const double` never does, so `const double kTick = 0.01;` can't feed a `constexpr` (`'kTick' was not declared 'constexpr'`). And g++ and clang accept `double copy[n]` with a run-time `n`, a C feature called a **variable-length array**. Clang warns, MSVC refuses, and standard C++ forbids it, so use a `std::vector` for a size you learn at run time. Writing `constexpr` whenever you mean "known while compiling" avoids both traps.

A `constexpr` value usually takes no memory at all. Below, `kLotSize` is `constexpr` and `lotSize` a plain global, both 100. This is g++ 10.2 at `-O0`, with no optimizer:

```text
_Z11sharesConsti:                         # return lots * kLotSize;
        ...
        mov     eax, DWORD PTR [rbp-4]
        imul    eax, eax, 100             # 100 sits inside the instruction
        ...
_Z9sharesVari:                            # return lots * lotSize;
        ...
        mov     eax, DWORD PTR lotSize[rip]   # loaded from memory on every call
        imul    eax, DWORD PTR [rbp-4]
        ...
```

Any code could change `lotSize`, so it must be read each time. Apple clang keeps no storage for `kLotSize` at all, and `nm` doesn't list it. A function can be `constexpr` too, so its result can size an array: *Compile-Time C++: constexpr, static_assert, and Type Traits*, in the advanced track, builds whole lookup tables that way.

example.title: A bid ladder and FIX messages
example.prompt: Size a ladder of bid prices with a constexpr depth, and name FIX message types with constexpr case labels.
example.output:
bids: 101.25 101.24 101.23 101.22
new order, execution report, unknown
example.explanation: `std::array<double, kDepth>` compiles because `kDepth` is `constexpr`: the 4 becomes part of the type, exactly as if you had typed `std::array<double, 4>`. Each `case` label must be a constant expression too, and `constexpr char` constants give FIX's one-letter message types readable names. In the Financial Information eXchange protocol, tag 35 says what a message is: `D` a new order, `F` a cancel, `8` an execution report. `best` is an ordinary `const`, since the loop only needs it at run time.

practice.title: A two-sided book
practice.prompt:
Hold both sides of a small book in one std::array sized by constexpr constants, and name FIX order types with constexpr case labels.

1. Declare `constexpr char kMarket = '1';`, `kLimit` as `'2'`, and `kStop` as `'3'`.
2. In `orderTypeName`, add a `case` for each one, returning `market`, `limit`, or `stop`.
3. Size `book` as `std::array<double, 2 * kLevels>`.
4. For each `i` below `kLevels`, set `book[i]` to `bestBid - i * kTickSize` and `book[kLevels + i]` to `bestAsk + i * kTickSize`.

Expected output:

```text
book: 49.95 49.90 49.85 50.00 50.05 50.10
market, limit, unknown
```
hints: `2 * kLevels` is itself a constant expression, because both parts are known while compiling.
Convert `i` with `static_cast<double>(i)` before multiplying by `kTickSize`, as the example does.

steps.title: Constants shared across files
steps.body:
The fee schedule lives in a header, `include/market.h`, which `fees.cpp`, `report.cpp`, and `main.cpp` include. How you declare it decides whether the program links, and how many copies of it ship. Recall from *Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker* that each `.cpp` gets its own pasted copy of the header's text.

A plain variable in a header is then defined once in every file that includes it, while the one definition rule from that lesson allows one per program. This is the Mac's linker with `double kFeeRate = 0.0005;` in the header:

```text
duplicate symbol '_kFeeRate' in:
    report.o
    fees.o
    main.o
ld: 1 duplicate symbols
```

A `const` or `constexpr` variable at namespace scope has **internal linkage**, as if it were marked `static`. Each file gets a private copy, so nothing clashes, and usually the copy costs nothing because the value is folded into the instructions. A table indexed at run time does need memory, though. With `constexpr std::array<double, 4> kFeeTiers` in the header, `nm` on a Mac finds a local copy in each object, lowercase like that lesson's `static` helpers (`_ZL` is how the compiler marks internal linkage in a name), and the program's read-only data holds 64 bytes, two copies of a 32-byte table:

```text
fees.o:   0000000000000018 s __ZL9kFeeTiers
report.o: 0000000000000020 s __ZL9kFeeTiers
```

C++17's **inline variable** fixes that: `inline constexpr std::array<double, 4> kFeeTiers = {...};`. As with an `inline` function, every file may define it, and the linker keeps one. `nm` now shows an external symbol, `S _kFeeTiers`, in both objects, `nm -m` calls it a `weak external` as it did that lesson's `inline` function, and the program holds 32 bytes. Make `inline constexpr` your default for a constant in a header.

The older way is `extern const double kRebate;` in the header, which only declares it, and `extern const double kRebate = 0.0002;` in exactly one `.cpp`. There's one copy, but the other files never see the value, so in them it isn't a constant expression (`std::array<double, kMaxLevels>` fails with `the value of 'kMaxLevels' is not usable in a constant expression`), and every use loads it from memory. What you gain is build time. Changing an `extern` value recompiles one file, while changing an `inline constexpr` recompiles every file that includes the header, a cost the next lesson, *Building Projects: Flags, Make, and CMake*, measures.

example.title: A fee schedule in a header
example.prompt: Share a lot size and a fee table through inline constexpr, and a rebate through extern const, in one file that stands in for a header and two .cpp files.
example.explanation: The sandbox runs one file, so the comments mark where each piece would live. In a real project the two `inline constexpr` lines and the two declarations sit in `market.h`, which both `.cpp` files include. `kFeeTiers.size()` is a constant expression wherever the header is included, so `main` can size an array with it. `kRebate` is defined once, in `fees.cpp`, and every other file sees only its declaration. A tier's fee is the notional, 101.25 times a lot of 100, times its rate, less the 2 basis point rebate: 10125 times 0.0008 is 8.1.

practice.title: Order size limits
practice.prompt:
Share order limits through a header's constants, then check orders against them.

1. Make `kLotSize` and `kMaxLotsByTier` `inline constexpr`, the right declaration for a header.
2. Finish `allowed`: an order is allowed only when `shares` is a whole number of lots, at most `kMaxLotsByTier[tier]` lots, and at most `kHardLimit` shares.
3. Leave `main` as it is. It prints each order with `ok` or `rejected`.

Expected output:

```text
1500 shares, tier 1: ok
1250 shares, tier 0: rejected
4500 shares, tier 0: rejected
400 shares, tier 2: ok
```

tests.output:
1500 shares, tier 1: ok
1250 shares, tier 0: rejected
4500 shares, tier 0: rejected
400 shares, tier 2: ok

hints: `shares % kLotSize == 0` is true for a whole number of lots.
Tier 0 allows 50 lots, which is 5,000 shares, but the hard limit of 4,000 still rejects 4,500.

steps.title: Enums and #define against constexpr
steps.body:
Before `constexpr`, code named its constants with the preprocessor or with enums, and you'll meet both in older codebases.

`#define TICK 0.01` is text replacement, and *The Preprocessor: Macros and Conditional Compilation* showed that a macro has no type and ignores scope. Here is what that does to a constant in someone else's namespace:

```cpp error
#include <iostream>

#define TICK 0.01

namespace futures {
    const double TICK = 0.25;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << futures::TICK << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

g++ sees `const double 0.01 = 0.25;` and says `error: expected unqualified-id before numeric constant`, with `note: in expansion of macro 'TICK'`. It's the same trap as the `min` and `max` macros of `<windows.h>`.

So macros get ALL_CAPS names, and nothing else should look like one. That's why most codebases, like *Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker* and the advanced lessons, name constants `kTickSize` rather than the UPPER_SNAKE_CASE of *Variables and Data Types*: no macro will ever be called `kTickSize`. Keep `#define` for what the preprocessor itself reads. `#if`, `#ifdef`, and `-D` flags act before the compiler runs, so they can't see a `constexpr`.

A plain **enum** names integer constants, but its names spill into the enclosing scope, and they turn into `int` without asking:

```cpp
enum LegacySide { Buy = 1, Sell = 2 };  // Buy and Sell are now global names
int oops = Buy + 7;                     // compiles, quietly an int
std::cout << oops << '\n';              // 8
```

The `enum class` from *Switch, enum class, and the Ternary Operator* keeps its names scoped and needs a `static_cast` to become a number. Give it an **underlying type** to choose its size and its values:

```cpp
enum class Side : char { Buy = '1', Sell = '2' };  // FIX tag 54's wire values
std::cout << static_cast<char>(Side::Sell) << ' ' << sizeof(Side) << '\n';  // 2 1
```

A function that takes a `Side` can't be handed a stray `'x'`, which a `char` parameter would accept. Old code also uses `enum { kDepth = 5 };` for an integer constant, from before `constexpr`. C++20 adds `consteval`, for a function that must run while compiling, and `constinit`, for a global whose starting value must be worked out while compiling, so no code has to run at startup to set it. The C++17 here has neither, and *What C++20 and C++23 Add*, in the advanced track, shows both.

example.title: FIX fields from enums
example.prompt: Build the side, order type, and quantity fields of a FIX new order from enum class values whose underlying type is char.
example.explanation: Each enum's values are FIX's own wire characters, so `static_cast<char>(Side::Buy)` is `'1'`, ready to send. FIX separates fields with a byte numbered 1, which logs show as `|`. The enums take one byte each, the size of a `char`. Because `newOrder` takes a `Side` and an `OrdType`, passing the two in the wrong order, or a bare `'1'`, is a compile error. With two `char` parameters, swapped arguments would compile, and the order would go out with its side and type mixed up.

practice.title: Time in force
practice.prompt:
Finish an enum class for FIX's time in force, tag 59, and print each value's field and meaning.

1. Add `Ioc = '3'` and `Fok = '4'` to `TimeInForce`.
2. Make `tifField` return `59=` followed by the enum's character. Start from `std::string("59=")`, since a bare literal plus a `char` isn't a string.
3. Add cases to `describe` returning `immediate or cancel` and `fill or kill`.
4. In `main`, print the same line for `Ioc` and for `Fok`, before the size line.

Expected output:

```text
59=0 day
59=1 good till cancel
59=3 immediate or cancel
59=4 fill or kill
size 1
```

tests.output:
59=0 day
59=1 good till cancel
59=3 immediate or cancel
59=4 fill or kill
size 1

hints: `static_cast<char>(tif)` gives the character the enum value was declared with.
`std::string("59=") + c` appends one `char` to a string.

recap:
- `const` means the value can't change through this name. It may still come from run time, like a limit computed at the start of the day.
- `constexpr` means the compiler computes the value, and the build fails where it can't. Array sizes, `std::array` sizes, and `case` labels need such constant expressions.
- A `const int` set from a literal counts as a constant, a `const double` doesn't, and `double a[n]` with a run-time `n` is a compiler extension. Use `constexpr`, and `std::vector` for run-time sizes.
- A `constexpr` value is usually folded into the instructions (`imul eax, eax, 100`), while a plain global is loaded from memory on every use.
- A namespace-scope `const` or `constexpr` has internal linkage, one private copy per file. `inline constexpr` (C++17) keeps one shared copy and is the default for a header.
- `extern const` in a header, defined in one `.cpp`, hides the value from other files, so it isn't a constant there, but changing it recompiles one file.
- Name constants `kName` and leave ALL_CAPS to macros. Keep `#define` for `#if` and `-D`.
- `enum class Side : char { Buy = '1' }` gives constants a type, a scope, and a size. A plain `enum` leaks its names and converts to `int`.

Next, **Building Projects: Flags, Make, and CMake** builds a many-file project the way teams do: the flags that matter, separate compilation, `make`, and CMake.
